title: Gastrointestinal Medications & Safety: Acid Control, Antiemetics, Motility and Bowel Therapy
html:
Gastrointestinal medications can relieve reflux, nausea, constipation, and diarrhea, but symptom suppression is not a diagnosis. The RN first looks for bleeding, obstruction, perforation, infection, dehydration, aspiration, electrolyte disturbance, medication toxicity, and acute abdominal deterioration. Safe care connects the drug to the suspected cause, the client’s organ function, and a measurable outcome.

Learning goals

  • Compare antacids, H2-receptor antagonists, proton pump inhibitors, and mucosal protectants.
  • Recognize important risks of antiemetics and prokinetic medications.
  • Select and evaluate bowel medications according to cause rather than symptom alone.
  • Avoid antimotility therapy when diarrhea may signal invasive infection, toxic megacolon, or obstruction.
  • Use lactulose and other hepatic-encephalopathy therapy safely.
  • Identify GI emergencies before administering a routine symptom medication.

Treat the cause, not just the symptom

Before giving a GI medication, assess onset, location and character of pain, distension, bowel sounds in context, nausea and emesis, stool pattern and appearance, oral intake, swallowing and aspiration risk, hydration, urine output, weight trend, vital signs, pregnancy status, recent surgery or travel, sick contacts, antibiotics, enteral feeding, alcohol and substance exposure, and all prescription and OTC products.

Hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, hematochezia with instability, rigid abdomen, rebound or guarding, sudden severe pain, persistent bilious or feculent vomiting, marked distension, absent passage of stool and gas, syncope, shock, or acute mental-status change requires urgent evaluation. Do not delay escalation by repeatedly administering antacids, antiemetics, laxatives, or antidiarrheals.

Symptom relief can hide deterioration
A lower nausea or pain score does not rule out bleeding, obstruction, ischemia, perforation, or infection. Reassess the abdomen, circulation, hydration, elimination, and overall trajectory.

Antacids act quickly but interact widely

Antacids neutralize existing acid and may relieve mild intermittent heartburn. Magnesium-containing products may cause diarrhea and accumulate with kidney impairment; aluminum- and calcium-containing products may cause constipation, and excess calcium-containing therapy can contribute to hypercalcemia or kidney injury. Sodium-containing products can worsen fluid or blood-pressure problems in susceptible clients.

Antacids can change gastric pH or bind other medicines, reducing absorption. Separate them from interacting medications according to current product information and pharmacy guidance. Persistent or frequent symptoms, dysphagia, weight loss, anemia, vomiting, or GI bleeding requires evaluation rather than continued self-treatment.

H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors reduce acid

H2-receptor antagonists reduce acid secretion. Some require renal dose adjustment, and older or acutely ill clients may develop confusion. Verify the exact agent because interaction profiles differ.

Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) suppress acid more strongly and are used for conditions such as GERD, erosive disease, ulcer treatment, and parts of selected GI-bleeding regimens. Give the exact formulation at the prescribed time; many products work best before food and delayed-release forms must not be crushed unless product instructions allow an alternative method.

Use the lowest appropriate regimen for the indicated duration and periodically confirm the indication. Longer or higher-dose exposure has been associated with risks that can include Clostridioides difficile infection, low magnesium, vitamin B12 deficiency, fractures, kidney injury, and drug interactions. These associations do not mean a needed PPI should be stopped abruptly without review.

Mucosal protectants and ulcer therapy require timing

Sucralfate forms a protective barrier and can bind other medications. It generally requires an empty stomach and separation from interacting drugs according to the order and product information. Constipation is common, and aluminum accumulation is a concern in severe kidney impairment. If administered through an enteral tube, verify formulation, tube compatibility, feeding separation, and flushing with pharmacy and local policy.

Helicobacter pylori eradication uses a complete multidrug regimen. Reinforce adherence, verify allergies and interactions, and do not substitute partial therapy. Bismuth can darken stool and tongue, but dark stool must still be distinguished from melena using symptoms, hemodynamics, hemoglobin trend, and clinical context.

Antiemetics have different mechanisms and hazards

Identify the likely cause of nausea: medication, postoperative state, vestibular disorder, migraine, pregnancy, chemotherapy, infection, obstruction, metabolic disturbance, increased intracranial pressure, or cardiac ischemia. Correct dehydration and electrolyte losses while treating symptoms.

Ondansetron and related 5-HT3 antagonists can prolong the QT interval, especially with congenital long-QT syndrome, bradyarrhythmia, low potassium or magnesium, heart disease, higher exposure, or other QT-prolonging drugs. Monitor risk factors and report palpitations, syncope, or dysrhythmia. Constipation and headache are common; serotonergic toxicity is possible with interacting drugs.

Promethazine and other sedating antiemetics can impair consciousness, breathing, blood pressure, and mobility. Promethazine injection can cause severe tissue injury with inadvertent arterial administration or extravasation; follow route-specific labeling and policy. Anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision, constipation, and confusion.

Metoclopramide requires movement surveillance

Metoclopramide promotes upper-GI motility and also treats nausea in selected conditions. It is contraindicated when stimulating motility could be dangerous, such as mechanical obstruction, perforation, or GI hemorrhage. Adjustments may be needed with kidney impairment.

Watch for acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, sedation, depression, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. The boxed warning addresses tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible; risk rises with treatment duration and cumulative exposure. Report repetitive oral, facial, trunk, or limb movements promptly and avoid treatment beyond the labeled duration unless the prescriber documents a rare benefit-over-risk exception.

New restlessness may be akathisia
Do not assume pacing, inability to sit still, or distress after metoclopramide is anxiety. Hold further exposure as appropriate, assess for extrapyramidal effects, and notify the prescriber.

Constipation therapy follows the mechanism

Assess last bowel movement, usual pattern, stool form, flatus, pain, distension, vomiting, diet and fluids, mobility, neurologic disease, recent surgery, rectal status, kidney and heart function, and constipating drugs such as opioids, anticholinergics, iron, calcium, and some antihypertensives. Suspected obstruction, impaction, acute abdomen, or toxic megacolon requires evaluation before a laxative.

  • Bulk-forming agents require adequate fluid and are unsafe when swallowing, fluid intake, severe narrowing, or obstruction is a concern.
  • Osmotic agents draw water into the bowel; monitor hydration and electrolytes. Magnesium products can accumulate in kidney impairment.
  • Stimulant laxatives increase motility and may cause cramping; they are used intentionally in selected regimens, including opioid-related constipation.
  • Stool softeners may help avoid straining in selected clients but do not rapidly treat impaction.
  • Rectal products require assessment for neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, rectal surgery, active bleeding, inflammation, or institutional restrictions.

Evaluate passage of stool and flatus, comfort, abdominal findings, hydration, electrolytes, and adverse effects. Diarrhea after a laxative does not prove that impaction or obstruction has resolved; liquid stool may pass around retained stool.

Diarrhea treatment begins with hydration and cause

Assess frequency, volume, blood or mucus, fever, pain, travel, food exposure, sick contacts, antibiotics, hospitalization, immunocompromise, tube feeding, medications, weight, orthostasis, mucous membranes, urine output, kidney function, and electrolytes. Use infection precautions and obtain stool testing when ordered.

Loperamide slows intestinal motility and can reduce selected noninvasive diarrhea, but avoid or obtain explicit clinical guidance when there is bloody stool, high fever, suspected invasive bacterial infection, C. difficile, acute ulcerative colitis flare, toxic megacolon, ileus, or significant distension. Excessive doses or interactions can cause life-threatening QT prolongation, ventricular dysrhythmias, syncope, and cardiac arrest.

Bismuth subsalicylate can interact with anticoagulants and other salicylates and is unsuitable for some clients with bleeding risk, salicylate allergy, kidney disease, pregnancy considerations, or viral illness in children and adolescents. It may harmlessly darken the tongue and stool, but never use that expectation to dismiss possible bleeding.

Hepatic encephalopathy: evaluate the brain and the bowel

Lactulose traps ammonia in the colon and promotes elimination in hepatic encephalopathy. Titrate only to the ordered clinical target, commonly a specified number of soft stools rather than uncontrolled diarrhea. Track mental status, asterixis, stool frequency, hydration, sodium and potassium, skin integrity, aspiration risk, and precipitating factors such as infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration, kidney injury, sedatives, and missed doses.

Improvement in an ammonia value alone is not the endpoint; evaluate cognition, safety, function, and the precipitating cause. Excess diarrhea can produce dehydration, hypernatremia or hypokalemia and worsen the client. Rifaximin may be added for selected recurrent disease; verify allergy, adherence, and access without treating it as a substitute for investigating deterioration.

Pancreatic enzymes and bile-related medications

Pancrelipase is taken with meals and snacks to support digestion in pancreatic insufficiency. Swallow delayed-release capsules intact or follow exact product instructions for opening and mixing; do not crush enteric-coated microspheres. Assess weight, stool quality, nutrition, glucose, mouth irritation, and dose-related adverse effects.

Ursodiol is used for selected cholestatic or gallstone conditions, not acute biliary obstruction. Monitor the prescribed liver tests and clinical response. Sudden right-upper-quadrant pain with fever, jaundice, hypotension, or confusion may indicate an obstructive or infectious emergency requiring urgent source control.

Medication administration through feeding tubes

Confirm tube location and route, use an enteral—not IV—connector, stop feeding when required, give each compatible medication separately, and flush before, between, and after medications according to the client’s fluid plan and policy. Never mix all drugs together or add them directly to formula. Do not crush enteric-coated, sublingual, hazardous, or extended-release products. Ask pharmacy for a safe formulation and specific feed-hold interval when absorption or binding is a concern.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify pain, bleeding, vomiting, stool pattern, distension, flatus, hydration, weight, vital signs, mental status, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, ECG risk, recent antibiotics, surgery, and all OTC products.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish uncomplicated reflux, medication adverse effect, constipation, infection, impaction, obstruction, bleeding, perforation, dehydration, dysrhythmia, extrapyramidal toxicity, or hepatic encephalopathy.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Shock, perforation, obstruction, aspiration, severe dehydration, toxic megacolon, major bleeding, ventricular dysrhythmia, and acute neurologic change require urgent action.
  4. Generate solutions: Hold unsafe symptom medication, protect airway and circulation, replace fluid and electrolytes as prescribed, obtain targeted tests, use precautions, review interactions, and involve the prescriber, pharmacist, GI team, or rapid response.
  5. Take action: Give the correct product, formulation, route, and timing; protect feeding-tube safety; stop harmful exposure; and escalate red flags.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess symptoms, abdominal findings, stool and emesis, hydration, urine output, electrolytes, ECG, movement, cognition, nutrition, function, and adverse effects.

Clinical example

A client receiving antibiotics develops frequent watery diarrhea, fever, abdominal tenderness, leukocytosis, and rising creatinine. A PRN loperamide order is available. The RN recognizes possible C. difficile infection with dehydration rather than routine diarrhea, holds the antimotility drug, initiates appropriate precautions, notifies the provider, obtains ordered stool testing, monitors perfusion and electrolytes, and begins prescribed fluid support. The RN continues to assess for ileus, distension, hypotension, and toxic megacolon.
